sections.title_en: 1. The Scribe Who Is Fit to Write
sections.body_en:
The Torah was given to all Israel, men and women alike, but the work of writing STaM – Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot – was placed upon the men, who were commanded to put on tefillin. As it is said (Devarim 6:8-9): "And you shall bind them for a sign upon your hand, and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes. And you shall write them upon the doorposts of your house and upon your gates"; the Sages expounded (Gittin 45b): "Whoever is included in binding is included in writing, and whoever is not included in binding is not included in writing". Therefore, women, who are not obligated in binding (putting on) tefillin, do not write tefillin and mezuzot, and likewise they do not write Torah scrolls, which are learned from tefillin by a gezera shava (the Rosh). And so is the law of minors and gentiles, who are not fit to write STaM.

A Jew who is a 'mumar' or a 'moser' – is unfit to write STaM (Gittin 45b; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 39:1; Yoreh De'ah 281:3). A 'mumar' is a Jew who has cast off the yoke of the mitzvot. And even if he cast off the yoke of the mitzvot for his own pleasure without wishing to provoke, since he has removed himself from the mitzvot as a whole, he is not among those who bind tefillin, and he has disqualified himself from being a STaM scribe. A 'moser' is a Jew who betrays his people and hands over his brothers or their property to tyrannical gentiles. And even if he keeps mitzvot, by his decision to betray his people he has removed himself from the community of Israel and from the Torah, and has disqualified himself from writing STaM.

A Jew who worships idols is also called a 'mumar' and is unfit to write STaM, and even if he keeps some of the mitzvot, since he worships idols he has removed himself from the community of Israel who are obligated in God's mitzvot. Likewise, one who commits a single transgression out of spite and in public, even if he keeps other mitzvot, since he has decided to perform an act of defiance against the faith and the Torah, is called a 'mumar' and is unfit to write STaM.1

notes_en.en:
In Gittin (45b) the views of the Tanna'im were brought regarding the law of a Torah scroll written by a gentile: "One taught: It is to be burned; and another taught: It is to be put in geniza; and another taught: One may read from it". From Rashi's words (there, s.v. 'Ve-amrei lah') it emerges that the halakha follows the view that holds that a Torah scroll written properly by a gentile may be read from. But the other Rishonim disagreed with him and held that a Torah scroll written by a gentile is invalid, because the gentile is not commanded to put on tefillin (Tosafot, Rambam, Ramban, Rosh and others; and so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 39:1; Yoreh De'ah 281:1). And some explain that Rashi too agrees with this, but he was explaining the view of the one who validates it (Beit Yosef, Yoreh De'ah 281:1; Erekh Ha-Shulḥan, Oraḥ Ḥayim 39:4).
Some hold that all the books written by those unfit to write must be put in geniza and it is forbidden to keep them, lest people think they are valid and come to stumble (Radbaz 2:774; Taz, Yoreh De'ah 281:1; Ḥatam Sofer, Gittin 45b). And some hold that although they are unfit for public reading, it is permitted to study in them (Erekh Ha-Shulḥan, Oraḥ Ḥayim 39:4; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan, Yoreh De'ah 281:4-5). And so that people will not err in them, one must mark on their parchment that they are invalid (Benei Yona 281:9), or on their 'etz ḥayim' (roller) (Nekudot Ha-Kesef, Yoreh De'ah 281:1).
See above 8, note 6, that according to the Derisha (281:1) a woman is fit to write a Torah scroll, but his view was rejected by most poskim. The poskim disagreed whether a woman is fit to write a Megillat Esther, as brought in Peninei Halakha, Zemanim 15, note 10.
One who treats the mitzva of tefillin with contempt, and even when he has time to put on tefillin does not want to put them on, is unfit to write STaM. And although he has no intention to spite or provoke, and he keeps many mitzvot, and therefore with regard to the rest of the Torah he is not considered a 'mumar', since he estranges himself from the mitzva of tefillin, he has removed himself from it, and is unfit to write STaM (Magen Avraham 39:3; Mishna Berura 6).

sections.body_en:
The scribe must be God-fearing and upright, because the validity of the writing depends on many laws that only the scribe knows whether he fulfilled. For example, if he forgets to have the intention of writing for the sake of the sanctity of the Torah scroll, the tefillin or the mezuza, or forgets to have the intention of writing one of the Divine Names for the sake of the sanctity of the Name – his writing is invalid (below halakha 7), and the proofreader or the buyer has no way of knowing this. Likewise, if he made a mistake in writing the passages of tefillin or a mezuza and corrected them out of their order – they are invalid (below halakha 15), and this too is not noticeable from outside. And then, if he sells invalid tefillin, it turns out that the one who buys from him will put on invalid tefillin every day and will not fulfil his mitzva. And if he did this with a mezuza, it turns out that the one who buys from him will live in a house without a mezuza (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:20). Therefore, a God-fearing scribe whose writing is average is preferable to a scribe whose writing is beautiful but about whom there is a concern that he has betrayed his trust (see above 4:13).

The scribe must write with great responsibility, for if he added one letter or omitted one letter, or even one part of a letter like the thorn of a 'yod', the Torah scroll is invalid (Menaḥot 29a). Likewise, there are words that are written in full spelling and some in defective spelling, and if he changed them – it is invalid (Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 275:6). It is told of Rabbi Yishmael that he said to his student Rabbi Meir, who earned his living by writing Torah scrolls: "My son, be careful in your work, for your work is the work of Heaven; perhaps you will omit one letter or add one letter – and you will be found destroying the whole world" (Eruvin 13a). For sometimes the change of a letter changes the meaning of the sentence in a way that creates blasphemy against Heaven, for example if instead of (Yirmeyahu 10:10): "But the Lord God is truth (emet)" he wrote: 'dead (met)' (Rashi). The Maharal added (Tiferet Yisrael 67) that the Torah is the spiritual root of the world, as the Sages said (Bereshit Rabba 1:1) that the Holy One, blessed be He, looked into the Torah and created the world according to it; it follows that every change of a letter in the Torah harms the spiritual root of the world, and thereby causes destruction.

So that the scribe will not make a mistake, the Sages forbade him to write even one letter of the Torah scroll not from a written text, and therefore he must place before him an accurate book (tikkun soferim), and copy from it precisely (Megilla 18b; Keset Ha-Sofer 4:5). In addition, the poskim ruled that the scribe should read every word aloud before he writes it (Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 274:2). If he transgressed and wrote not from a written text, some say that from the outset one should not read from the scroll without a thorough proofreading of the part he wrote from memory (Beit Yosef there; the Rashba and the Ḥiddushei Ha-Rim, Megilla there).

A scribe for whom the passages of tefillin and mezuza are fluent, since they are short and familiar, may write them not from a written text while uttering every word before he writes it. But the choicest way of performing the mitzva is that he too should write them from a written text (Megilla there; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:29, 31; Mishna Berura 134, 136).

Many scribes today write from a written text by means of transparencies and a 'light table'. The scribe places on the 'light table' a transparency of the column of the Torah scroll, and over it he places the parchment precisely, and because of the light the transparency is seen through the parchment, so that the scribe reads from the transparency and copies directly onto the parchment, without concern that he will make a mistake.

The scribe must write with the hand with which he usually writes, that is, the right hand, and a left-handed person – with the left hand. And if he wrote with a hand with which he does not usually write – it is invalid, because the mitzva is to write in the normal manner of writing and not in an unusual way; just as one who writes on Shabbat with his left hand does not transgress a Torah prohibition and is not liable to a sin-offering (the Teruma 205; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:5; Yoreh De'ah 271:7).

It is a mitzva to write a beautiful and straight script, as it is said (Shemot 15:2): "This is my God and I will glorify Him" – "Beautify yourself before Him in mitzvot" (Shabbat 133b; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 274:3). From the period of the Aḥaronim a pious custom began to spread among scribes to immerse for a seminal emission before writing (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:42. See Peninei Halakha, Simḥat Ha-Bayit U-Virkhato 3:9).

It is a law given to Moshe at Sinai that Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot must be written on the processed hide of animals. If he wrote them on paper or cloth or on hide that is not processed, they are invalid (Shabbat 79b). The parchment must be from the hide of kosher domestic animals, wild animals or birds, but the hides of non-kosher animals that are forbidden to eat are unfit for writing STaM, as it is said (Shemot 13:9): "that the Torah of the Lord may be in your mouth"; the Sages expounded – "from what is permitted in your mouth". Hides of animals of kosher species that died without shekhita or were tereifa are also valid, for the main thing is that they be of a species fit to be eaten. One does not write sacred writings on the skin of kosher fish, because it has filth in it (Shabbat 108a; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:12; Yoreh De'ah 271:1).

Parchment is the most durable natural material on which one can write properly. In addition, it is the most elevated material for writing, for all papers are made from kinds of plants, whereas parchment is made from the animal kingdom, which is above the level of plants. At the same time, the vitality of animals is a coarse physical vitality devoid of understanding, and the hide is the outer part of that vitality. By writing the Torah on the hides of animals, we learn that the Torah illuminates and guides the whole world, even the outer side of the enormous forces of life that appear animal-like and without understanding.

It is a law given to Moshe at Sinai that STaM must be written on processed hide. The Sages said that there are three stages of processing: salting, flouring and treating with gall-nuts (Shabbat 79a).
a) Salting – the hide is placed in salt in order to draw out of it the juices and acids that cause it to rot. At this stage the hide is also soaked in lime so that it will shed its hair. b) Flouring – the hide is soaked in water with barley flour, whose fermentation widens the pores in preparation for absorbing the gall-nut water. At this stage it is called 'diftera' and is unfit for STaM, because it is not strong and taut, and the ink tends to smear on it. c) Treating with gall-nuts – the hide is soaked in water with ground gall-nuts, until the hide becomes strong and taut. The processing must be for the sake of the sanctity of a Torah scroll, as will be explained below (halakha 6).

In the days of the exile, in Spain and in Ashkenaz, people began to carry out the whole processing to its completion with lime instead of gall-nuts. There were Geonim who disqualified these hides for STaM, but the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim ruled that the main thing is that the hide come out processed in such a way that the writing will be absorbed well by the hide, and therefore the status of processing with lime is equal to processing with gall-nuts (Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 271:2).2

notes_en.en: Processing with gall-nuts is explained in the Gemara, Shabbat (79a), and in the Rambam (Tefillin 1:6). In the Responsa of the Rambam (153) he added that if the scroll was processed with lime – it is invalid, but after the fact one may read from it with a blessing, because in his view one may after the fact recite a blessing over an invalid scroll (below 15:18, note 18). And so it is brought in the Responsa of the Geonim (Harkavy 63), that it is invalid. On the other hand, Rabbeinu Tam wrote (Shabbat 79b; Maḥzor Vitry, siman 517) that our processing with lime is good and strong and is considered like processing with gall-nuts, for the main thing is that it be possible to write on it in the most fitting manner. And so ruled the great majority of the Rishonim, among them: the Or Zarua, the Ramban, the Rosh, the Ran, the Ritva and the Me'iri. And so is the view of Rav Moshe Gaon (Responsa of the Geonim, Harkavy 432). And so it was ruled in the Tur and the Shulḥan Arukh (Yoreh De'ah 271:2), the Mishna Berura (32:23), the Kol Ya'akov 34, and others. And so is the custom of the great majority of scribes in the Land, except for some of the immigrants from Yemen. In the Diaspora people were accustomed to process with gall-nuts in other communities in Islamic lands too. Apparently, they switched to processing with lime because processing with it is quicker, easier and cheaper. The colour of hide processed with lime is white and the colour of hide processed with gall-nuts is reddish-brown, and some were accustomed to add turmeric to make it yellowish, and since it only gives appearance, it does not invalidate (Sa'arat Teiman, p. 99). Simply, for members of all communities there is an enhancement in using hide treated with gall-nuts, but in practice only very few are particular about this.

sections.body_en:
There are three kinds of hide for writing: gevil, kelaf and dukhsustos. The whole hide is called gevil, and it can be divided in two – the outer part (the epidermis) is called kelaf, and the inner part (the dermis) is called dukhsustos. Gevil is valid for writing Torah scrolls and mezuzot and invalid for tefillin, and one must write on its outer side, where the hair was. Dukhsustos is valid for writing a mezuza only, and one must write on the side facing the hair. Kelaf is valid for tefillin, Torah scrolls and mezuzot, that is, it is the only one valid for all the sacred writings, and one must write on its inner side. If he deviated and wrote on kelaf on its outer side, or on gevil and dukhsustos on their inner side – it is invalid. The basis of these laws is a law given to Moshe at Sinai.

But according to several of the greatest Rishonim, the places of kelaf and dukhsustos are reversed. Seemingly, according to this there is no way to satisfy all the views, for tefillin must be written only on kelaf, and the question is what kelaf is. But in practice, according to the custom accepted since the days of the Rishonim to scrape the whole hide (the gevil) on both its sides and to prepare its writing surface on the inner side, it turns out that what we are left with is kelaf that is valid according to all views for Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot, as explained in the note.3

notes_en.en:
An animal's hide is divided into two layers: the thin outer part is called the epidermis, and the thick inner part is called the dermis. In the language of the Sages, the whole hide is called 'gevil', and when its thickness is split in two – the outer part is called 'kelaf' and the inner 'dukhsustos'. The Sages said (Shabbat 79b): It is a law given to Moshe at Sinai that on gevil and dukhsustos one writes on the outer side, towards the hair, and on kelaf one writes on its inner side, towards the flesh. They further said there that if he wrote on the other side it is invalid, and Rabbi Aḥa validates it. They further said that it is a law given to Moshe at Sinai that a Torah scroll is written on gevil, tefillin on kelaf, and a mezuza on dukhsustos (Menaḥot 32a; Yerushalmi Megilla 1:9; Massekhet Soferim 1:5; Rambam, Tefillin 1:8). The Rishonim explained that tefillin are valid only on kelaf, a Torah scroll is valid only on gevil and kelaf, and a mezuza is valid on all three kinds (Rambam, Tefillin 1:9; the Rosh, the Ran, the Teruma, and others. Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:7; Yoreh De'ah 271:3; 288:6). And some say that a Torah scroll is valid also on dukhsustos (Tanna de-Vei Menashe, Shabbat 79b; and so wrote the Rosh, the Ran, the Teruma and the Tur, brought in the Beit Yosef 271:3). And some say that a mezuza is invalid on gevil (the Ri in Tosafot). To sum up, only kelaf is valid for tefillin, a Torah scroll and a mezuza.
As mentioned, if he changed the side of writing it is invalid, except that the Rishonim disagreed about the definition of kelaf and dukhsustos. According to most Rishonim, kelaf is the outer part (the epidermis) and one must write on its inner side, and dukhsustos is the inner part (the dermis) and one must write on the side facing the hair; and in their view it is fitting to write in this way, on the side that does not actually touch the flesh or the hair (Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafot, Shabbat 79b; Rabbeinu Ḥananel, the Ittur, the Semag, the Rosh, the Mordekhai, the Hagahot Maimoniyot, the Yere'im, the Teruma). And so it was ruled in the Shulḥan Arukh (Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:7). On the other hand, some say that kelaf is the inner part, and one must write on the side that touched the flesh, and dukhsustos is the outer part and one must write on the hair side. And in their view this is more natural – to write on the outer edge of the hide, or on the side that touches the flesh or the hair (Rav Hai Gaon; Rambam, Tefillin 1:7, and in the Responsa of the Rambam 289; the Ittur, the Ramban, the Rashba and the Ritva).
Simply, regarding tefillin, which must be written on kelaf, the dispute is polar and there is no way to satisfy both views, for according to Rabbeinu Tam and most poskim one must write on the outer part (the epidermis) on its inner side, and according to the Rambam one must write on the inner part (the dermis) on its inner side. But as will be explained, in practice one satisfies both views:
Already in the period of the Rishonim many were accustomed not to split the hide (the gevil) in two, but processed and scraped the hide on both its sides, and the Rishonim explained (Rabbeinu Tam, the Rosh, the Mordekhai, the Me'iri, the Ran and others) that these hides have the law of 'kelaf', since a significant layer was removed from the side facing the flesh, and consequently the name dukhsustos no longer applies to it, and one writes on the inner side facing the flesh, according to the view of Rabbeinu Tam and most poskim. And so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh (Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:7). However, some poskim warned not to remove the whole thin outer layer (the epidermis), for if the whole of it is removed – the name kelaf no longer applies to it, and its law is like dukhsustos, which is invalid for tefillin and a Torah scroll (Nishmat Adam 14; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 32:20). The problem is that in practice the whole thin outer layer (the epidermis) is often removed. But several of the greatest Rishonim explained that even if the whole of it was removed, since much was also removed from the side facing the flesh, it no longer has the law of dukhsustos but its law is like kelaf. So wrote the Rosh (Laws of Torah Scroll 5), the Teruma and the Me'iri. And so wrote the Ḥatam Sofer (Oraḥ Ḥayim 3) in practice. And so emerges from the words of the Rishonim who will be brought below, who hold that the main difference between gevil and kelaf depends on the side that was prepared for writing: if the inner side was prepared for writing – it is kelaf.
This kelaf of ours is valid also according to the Rambam and those with him, for if the whole epidermis was removed, then in his view what remains is choice kelaf, and one writes on the inner side facing the flesh, as the halakha is in his view. But seemingly, if a little of the epidermis was left, it is no longer kelaf but gevil, and invalid for tefillin. However, several of the poskim who follow the Rambam's view, foremost among them the Ritva (Shabbat 79b) in the name of the Ra'ah, explained that even if he did not remove the outer layer, as long as he prepared the side facing the flesh for writing, its law is like kelaf and not like gevil, for the definition of gevil is that it was prepared for writing on the hair side, and the definition of kelaf is that it was prepared for writing on the side facing the flesh (the Ḥiddushim attributed to the Ran, Shabbat 79b; Ḥatam Sofer, Oraḥ Ḥayim 3. And so explained Rav Idua Elba in his book 'Gevil Ve-Kelaf'). And it seems that this is what all the Rishonim meant who defined gevil as 'not prepared on the flesh side', that is, not made fit for writing on the flesh side. Thus it emerges that our parchments are valid according to both views, and according to all views one must write on their inner side facing the flesh.
Today people are accustomed to write everything on kelaf (as it is called in our speech, that is, scraped on both sides). For it is the strongest and most convenient for writing, and they prefer the enhancement of beautiful parchment and beautiful writing over the enhancement of a Torah scroll on gevil and a mezuza on dukhsustos (Rema, Yoreh De'ah 271:3; Shulḥan Gavoha 19; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 21-22). Only individuals are particular to write a Torah scroll on gevil and a mezuza on dukhsustos.

sections.body_en:
It is a law given to Moshe at Sinai that one must score the upper line of all the lines in Torah scrolls and mezuzot before writing them. If he erred and wrote without scoring, even if he succeeded in writing as straight as a ruler – it is invalid. And even if he scores after the writing it will not help, since he wrote without scoring. The scoring must be done by means of a scratch made on the parchment with a stylus (a blunt knife), and not with a pen or a pencil that leaves colour on the parchment (Menaḥot 32b; Rambam, Tefillin 1:12; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 271:5).

From the outset it is good to score for the sake of the mitzva of writing a Torah scroll or a mezuza, but if he scored not for its sake – it is valid (Bei'ur Halakha 32:8, s.v. 'Bi-teḥillat'). From the outset one also scores the sides, in order to help the scribe straighten the lines at their beginning and their end (Rema, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:6).

Tefillin do not need scoring, because the passages of the tefillin are covered by the leather of the boxes, and therefore there is no particular insistence that they be written in a straight line as in a Torah scroll (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:6). But by rabbinic law one must score the first line, and according to it the scribe will straighten the rest of the lines. For the Sages ruled regarding all verses that, out of respect for them, anyone who comes to write three or more words of a verse should score the first line, so that he will not write them crooked (Gittin 6b; Rambam, Tefillin 7:16; above 8:10). And one should not be stringent to score all the lines, because the Sages said (Yerushalmi Shabbat 1:2): "Whoever is exempt from something and does it – is called a commoner (hedyot)". But if he wants to score all the lines in order to write the tefillin in a more beautiful script, he is not called a commoner, since he does not do so as an obligation out of error, but in order to beautify the script (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:8). And so is the custom.

There were scribes who were accustomed to coat the parchment with a kind of white coating, in order to beautify the parchment and to ease the drawing of the quill. Some say that there is an enhancement of the mitzva in this, because by this means the writing is more beautiful, and anything that comes to beautify the writing does not constitute an interposition (Penei Me'irot 3:32). But if the parchment is coated with a thick layer, it tends to crumble over time and the letters on it crack and fall off. Therefore one must pass a cloth over the coated parchment and wipe it well, in order to remove what is not well stuck, and what remains becomes one mass with the parchment and does not constitute an interposition (Sha'arei Teshuva, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:6). On the other hand, some say that this coating constitutes an interposition, and only if the ink passes through the white coating and is absorbed into the parchment, so that even if the coating is peeled off the letters will remain on the parchment – is the scroll valid. But if when the coating is peeled off the ink will fall off – the scroll is invalid (Benei Yona).

In practice, since the matter is disputed, one should not use coated parchments (Keset Ha-Sofer 2:12). But one should not refrain from reading from a coated Torah scroll and reciting the blessing over it, for some hold that one may recite the blessing even over an invalid Torah scroll (below 15:18). But regarding tefillin and mezuzot one must be stringent, for according to all views one does not fulfil the obligation with invalid passages (Yeḥaveh Da'at 6:55). In addition, when rolling the passages in order to insert them into the boxes, there is a concern that the coating will crack and the letters will become invalid.

One must process the hide for the sake of the mitzva one intends to fulfil with it, and if he did not process the hide for the sake of the mitzva – it is invalid (Gittin 54b). Therefore, one must say at the beginning of the processing: "I am processing these hides for the sake of a Torah scroll", or "for the sake of tefillin", or "for the sake of a mezuza". If he processed the parchment for the sake of a mezuza – it is invalid for tefillin, for the sanctity of tefillin is more severe than the sanctity of a mezuza. If he processed it for the sake of tefillin – it is invalid for a Torah scroll, for the sanctity of a Torah scroll is more severe than the sanctity of tefillin. But if he processed it for the sake of a Torah scroll, it is valid for tefillin or for mezuzot; therefore people are accustomed always to process for the sake of a Torah scroll.

It is forbidden to make mundane use of parchment that was processed for the sake of writing STaM. And if one estimates that perhaps there will be a need to use the remnants of the hide for mundane purposes, such as for writing a get or for practising STaM writing, one may add a condition, and say: "I am processing these hides for the sake of a Torah scroll, and I stipulate that if I wish – I may change them for any purpose", and by this means they may be used also for mundane purposes (Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 271:1; Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:8; Mishna Berura 26-27). But if he began to write matters of holiness on the parchment, the condition he made no longer helps, and it is forbidden to use the rest of the parchment for mundane matters (Mishna Berura 42:23).

Since the processing must be for the sake of the mitzva, it must be carried out by a Jew. In a pressing situation, the processing may be done by a gentile, on condition that a Jew is present at the beginning of the processing and tells the gentile to have in mind the sake of a Torah scroll, and also participates with him in putting the hide into the lime (Shulḥan Arukh and Rema, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:9).

The writing of STaM must be for the sake of the sanctity of STaM. Therefore, before beginning to write the Torah scroll the scribe must say: "I am writing this scroll for the sake of the sanctity of a Torah scroll". And so is the law regarding tefillin and a mezuza, that before writing them one must say: "for the sake of the sanctity of tefillin" or "for the sake of the sanctity of a mezuza". If he wrote even one letter before saying this, the scroll or the passages are invalid. The statement the scribe makes at the beginning of the writing – is effective for the whole duration of the writing, even if it lasts years, for everything he writes he writes according to his first intention (Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 274:1; Keset Ha-Sofer 4:1). However, it is good that after every break, before he continues his writing, he say again the formula he said at the beginning (Mishna Berura 32:92; Kol Ya'akov 274:5). When another scribe needs to complete or correct the scroll or the passages, even by one letter, he is obligated to say that he is writing for the sake of their sanctity, for the first scribe's intention does not help him (Birkei Yosef, Yoreh De'ah 274:1; Mishna Berura 32:93-94; Keset Ha-Sofer 4:3).

In addition to the general intention for the sake of the sanctity of STaM, before writing each 'azkara', that is, a holy Name, the scribe is obligated to sanctify the azkara and to say: "for the sake of the sanctity of the Name". And if he did not sanctify the azkarot – it is invalid (Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 276:2. Below 11:3 it will be explained which are the holy Names). With Names about which there is doubt, he must stipulate that if they are holy he is writing them for the sake of the sanctity of the Name (Keset Ha-Sofer 10:7).

Because of the great sanctity of the Name, it is forbidden to stop in the middle of writing it, and even if the king of Israel greets him, he should not answer him. One who writes two or more holy Names in succession, such as in the verse (Devarim 6:4): "Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one" – one statement is effective for all of them. But if he needs to stop, he may stop between writing one Name and the next, and when he returns to write the second Name, he should say again: "for the sake of the sanctity of the Name" (Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 276:3).

From the outset it is good that before the writing the scribe say that he is writing all the azkarot for the sake of the sanctity of the Name. So that before writing a Torah scroll he should say: "I am writing this scroll for the sake of the sanctity of a Torah scroll, and all the azkarot in it for the sake of the sanctity of the Name", and he should add this also before writing tefillin or a mezuza (Mishna Berura 32:96).

After the fact, if when he wrote an azkara he was aware that he was writing a holy Name, and forgot to say before writing the Name: "for the sake of the sanctity of the Name" – it is valid, because the statement at the beginning of writing the scroll or the passages is effective to have the writing considered as being for the sake of the sanctity of the Name, together with this awareness (Maharsham 8:214).

If he erred and wrote an azkara in the wrong place or without intention, since it is impossible to erase the holy Name, there is no way to repair what he made crooked, and he must put the sheet or the passage in geniza. In a pressing situation people are lenient to cut out or to peel off the Name (as will be explained below in halakha 14). If he forgot where the holy Name is that he wrote in the Torah scroll without intention, the scroll is invalid without remedy (Keset Ha-Sofer 10:4).4

notes_en.en:
We learned in Gittin (45b) that one must write the Torah scroll for its own sake, for if according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel one must process for its own sake the hide from which the boxes of the tefillin are made, all the more so must one write it for its own sake. We further learned (there 54b) that a Torah scroll whose azkarot were not written for their own sake – is invalid. Some say that there is no need to have explicit intention for the scroll and the azkarot, for the ordinary writing of a Torah scroll and of azkarot is for the sake of the mitzva and the sanctity of the Name (one answer in Tosafot and in Tosafot of Sens, Avoda Zara 27a; Rabbeinu Elḥanan as brought in the Mordekhai, Menaḥot 949. And so wrote, after the fact, the Penei Me'irot 1:45). And some say that although the ordinary writing of a Torah scroll is for its own sake, before writing each of the azkarot one must have special intention (Rambam, as explained by the Mahari Asad and the Mikdash Me'at). But according to most Rishonim, one must have intention both in writing the scroll, that it be for its own sake, and in the azkarot, that they be for the sake of the sanctity of the Name (Rabbeinu Tam, the Semag, the Teruma, Tosafot, Avoda Zara 27a; the Ramban, the Rosh, the Mordekhai, the Me'iri, the Hagahot Maimoniyot and Rabbeinu Yeruḥam). And so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh (Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:19). According to most poskim, the obligation of intention in writing and in the azkarot is from the Torah (Tosafot; Levush 32:19; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 32:31; Responsa Yehuda Ya'aleh of Asad, part 1, Yoreh De'ah 269; Rav Gutmacher in Aderet Eliyahu, Yoreh De'ah 89; Divrei Yatziv, Yoreh De'ah 174). And according to the Peri Megadim (Oraḥ Ḥayim 32, Eshel Avraham 32), it is rabbinic.
Some say that if he did not say aloud at the beginning of the writing that he is writing for the sake of the sanctity of a Torah scroll but only thought it in his heart – it is not effective (Beit Yosef, Yoreh De'ah 276:1; Eliya Rabba, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:36; Peri Megadim; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 31; Mishna Berura 95; Kol Ya'akov 1, and others). And some say that it is effective after the fact (Radbaz 1:154; Rema of Fano 94; the Baḥ, Yoreh De'ah 276; Shakh 1; Benei Yona 274:1; Shulḥan Gavoha, Yoreh De'ah 271:8; Keset Ha-Sofer 4:1).
Regarding the azkarot, some say that sanctifying God's Names in thought is effective (the Rosh and the Tur). And some were in doubt about this (the Semag, the Teruma). And some hold that only a spoken statement is effective, and if he did not say it – it is invalid (Tosafot, Avoda Zara 27a; Orḥot Ḥayim, Tefillin 24), and so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh (Yoreh De'ah 276:2; and likewise the Beit Yosef, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:19). And the Yehuda Ya'aleh (part 1, Yoreh De'ah 269) explained that it is invalid rabbinically. After the fact, according to most poskim thought is effective for the azkarot too, once he has said aloud a statement for the whole scroll. So wrote the Rema (Oraḥ Ḥayim there), the Levush, the Baḥ (276:2), the Eliya Rabba, the Peri Megadim (Eshel Avraham 32:32), the Shakh (Yoreh De'ah 276:1), the Kol Ya'akov 1, the Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav (32:31) and the Mishna Berura (32:99). Some hold that this thought means that he wrote with knowledge and recognition that he was writing a holy Name (Benei Yona 276:2; Mikdash Me'at, rule 6:2). And some hold that he must stop and think that he is writing "for the sake of the sanctity of the Name" (Birkei Yosef 276:5; Mishbetzot Zahav 32:41). And some say that if at the beginning of the writing he sanctified all the azkarot, as the Taz advises (below), and forgot to sanctify an azkara aloud, he may be lenient like those who hold that writing with knowledge and recognition that it is a holy Name is sufficient (Maharsham 8:214).
The Taz wrote (274:1) that it is right for the scribe to say at the beginning of his writing: "I am writing this scroll for the sake of the sanctity of a Torah scroll, and all the azkarot in it for the sake of the sanctity of the Name", and it will be effective after the fact in case he forgets to have in mind the sanctity of the Name before writing one of the Names. And so wrote in practice the Ḥemed Moshe (Oraḥ Ḥayim 39:1), the Peri Megadim (Eshel Avraham 32:32), the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (276:2), the Avnei Nezer (Yoreh De'ah 359), the Yehuda Ya'aleh (Asad, part 1, Yoreh De'ah 269) and the Maharsham (1:156). But many disagree and hold that this is not effective: the Divrei Ḥamudot (Laws of Torah Scroll 3), the Davar Shmuel 76, the Eliya Rabba (32:19), the Benei Yona (276:1), the Birkei Yosef (Yoreh De'ah 276:3), the Lishkat Ha-Sofer (10:5), the Kol Ya'akov (274:4), and many others. In the Bei'ur Halakha (32:19) he decided that one may rely on the Taz when the scribe is in doubt whether he thought of the sanctity of the Name. Therefore people were accustomed to say so at the beginning of the writing (Mishna Berura 32:96; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 32:42; Mishnat Avraham of Yafeh 19:5).

sections.body_en:
It is a law given to Moshe at Sinai that the writing of STaM must be in ink (Yerushalmi Megilla 1:9). The definition of ink is that it is completely black and its colour is durable, but if its colour tends towards green or blue or red – it is invalid. If he wrote even one letter in a colour that is not black – it is invalid (Rambam, Tefillin 1:5; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:3; Yoreh De'ah 271:6). From the outset the ink should have another property, that it can be erased, and by this means letters in which a mistake occurred can be corrected. Therefore some ruled that one should not mix into the ink kankantom (vitriol), which is hard to erase (Eruvin 13a; Rambam there 1:4).

People were accustomed to prepare the ink from the soot of oils, pitch or wax, and in this way they created the black colour. In order that the soot stick well to the parchment they kneaded it with 'gum', that is, tree resin, and a little honey. Afterwards they would dry the mixture until it became wafers, and before writing they would dissolve the wafer in gall-nut water and write (Rambam, Tefillin 1:4-5). The drawback was that this ink did not adhere to the parchment with great durability, and sometimes tended to crumble and flake off the parchment. In order to create durable ink, people were accustomed to prepare ink from gall-nut water with kankantom and gum. 'Gall-nuts' are round growths formed on plants, especially on the oak tree, as a reaction to insect stings. The gall-nuts are ground and boiled, and in this way a solution rich in a substance called 'tannin' is obtained. Kankantom is iron sulphate. When kankantom is brought together with a liquid extract of gall-nuts, a shiny black colour is formed, which binds well to the parchment. It is mixed with the 'gum' in order to thicken it and make it adhere. In this way a very strong ink is created, and although it is hard to erase, it is valid. And even if it could not be erased at all, it would be valid after the fact (Rambam there; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 271:6; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 32:4).5

Sometimes it happens that the black colour fades and tends slightly towards a reddish-grey shade. Some say that the STaM writing is thereby invalidated, since its letters are not completely black. And in tefillin and mezuzot, which must be written in order, it is not possible to correct this by passing a quill with black ink over them (Peri Megadim; Keset Ha-Sofer 3:2; 9:9). But according to most poskim, STaM writing to which this happened is valid, since it was written in valid ink, and this is the way of the ink, that over time it takes on a reddish shade, and even then it is called black. But it is good to pass over it a quill with black ink (Ḥatam Sofer, Yoreh De'ah 256; Mishna Berura 32:128; Yaskil Avdi 5, Yoreh De'ah 53).

notes_en.en:
Eruvin (13a): according to Rabbi Yishmael one should not mix kankantom into the ink, for it is said in the passage of the sota (Bamidbar 5:23): "and he shall write… and he shall blot them out into the water of bitterness" – "a writing that can be blotted out", and ink with kankantom is not erased without leaving a mark. And according to Rabbi Meir only the passage of the sota may not be written with kankantom. And the Tanna'im disagreed whether in his view the prohibition applies only to the scroll of the sota written for a sota woman, or also to the passage of the sota in a Torah scroll. According to the Ritva (Eruvin 13a) in the name of the Ramban, in our time, when the Temple is destroyed, according to all views it is permitted to write the passage of the sota in a Torah scroll with kankantom. And according to the Ran, even in the time of the Temple the halakha follows the view that in a Torah scroll one may write with kankantom. And according to the Rambam (Tefillin 1:4; Responsa of the Rambam 136), ink with kankantom is valid, but the choicest way of performing the mitzva is to follow Rabbi Yishmael and not to mix kankantom in writing STaM. And some of the Rishonim disqualified mixing kankantom and gall-nuts into the ink, because they learned from the Gemara that it is not called 'ink' (Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafot, Gittin 19a, s.v. 'Deyo deyuta'; the Semag and the Teruma). But most Rishonim were not concerned for Rabbeinu Tam and agreed that it is permitted to mix gall-nuts into the ink (the Rosh, the Ran, Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, the Kesef Mishneh, and many others).
According to the Shulḥan Arukh (Yoreh De'ah 271:6), from the outset it is right to make the ink from the soot of oils, and the Rema added, based on the Zohar (part 2, Ra'aya Meheimna 159a), that the oils should come from wood. And one uses gum and gall-nuts (soot ink). But by the letter of the law, even if it is not from wood, it is valid.
In practice the Aḥaronim wrote that the prevalent custom is to mix kankantom into the ink, although it is not erasable and does not come from wood, because it is more durable. So wrote many, among them: the Beit Yosef (32:3), the Maharam Provinzalo 39, the Baḥ (271:6), the Benei Yona (271:17), the Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav (32:4), the Birkei Yosef (271:7), the Zekhor Le-Avraham (Yoreh De'ah 60), the Keset Ha-Sofer (3:1), the Mishna Berura (32:8) and the Kol Ya'akov (271:17). And some take extra care to write with ink from wood without kankantom (soot ink). And they claim that ink from kankantom reddens a little over the years. But most scribes write with ink with kankantom, because they are concerned that ink from soot may detach and flake off the parchment.
Scribes who wish to enhance the drawing of the crowns (tagin) may use a rapidograph, which is a very fine pen of graphic designers (Yeri'ot Shlomo, part 1, 3, note 7). For only ink made from things forbidden to eat is invalid, and in practice ink is not produced today from things forbidden to eat.

sections.body_en:
The STaM writings are written with the help of a quill that takes up the ink from the inkwell. All quills are valid, but many were accustomed to write with a quill made of a reed that grows beside a pool of water, which has softness and flexibility. The Sages said (Ta'anit 20b): "A person should always be soft like a reed and not hard like a cedar, and therefore the reed merited that a quill is taken from it to write with it a Torah scroll, tefillin and mezuzot". But as mentioned, all quills are valid, and in Ashkenaz people were accustomed to write with a quill made of a feather or of iron (Benei Yona 271:24; Keset Ha-Sofer 3:6). Today ceramic quills have been developed that are both strong and soft, and the writing with them is better. And since the main thing is that the writing be beautiful, it is preferable to use them.

After the invention of printing the question arose whether Torah scrolls may be written by means of printing (relief type). Some say that it is permitted, for printing is like stamping with a seal, which is considered writing. That is, the letters are raised and ink is put on them, and the scribe lowers them onto the parchment. In their view this action is considered writing, because there is no difference between bringing the ink down onto the parchment by means of a quill or by means of a seal. And there is even an advantage in this, that the printing letters were arranged precisely from a written text, and afterwards there will be no mistake in them. In addition, when the act of writing is done all at once, it is easier to have the intention, for one intention for the sake of the sanctity of the scroll and the sanctity of the Names will be effective for several columns, without there being time for extraneous thoughts to impair the intention. Regarding tefillin and mezuzot the problem is more difficult, for they must be written in order, and it is possible that in their view the permission to write them is only if they are written with a rotary press, letter after letter.

On the other hand, some say that a Torah scroll must be written by hand, as it is said (Devarim 31:19): "Now therefore write for yourselves", and the manner of writing is forming the letter by drawing the quill and not by means of a seal or printing. They further argued that even if we consider it a kind of writing, it is writing by 'grama' (indirect causation), that is, a person performed one action of lowering the type onto the sheet, and the writing is as though done by itself. And some added that one must have the intention 'for its own sake' before writing each of the Names, and here the intention is swallowed up within the writing of the whole sheet. They were further concerned that if printing were permitted, people unfit for writing STaM (above halakha 1) would also make scrolls, and invalid scrolls would multiply.

In practice, although about half of the poskim were lenient to write STaM by printing, since many hold that printing is invalid for writing STaM, and the laws of writing are from the Torah, one must be stringent.6

notes_en.en:
Engraving is not considered writing, as the Sages said regarding a get (Gittin 20a): "And he shall write – and not engrave". The Gemara there explained that the engraving that is not considered writing is only in the manner of 'ḥak tokhot', that is, erasing parts of a blot of ink, so that the engraving is done around the letter, and the letter is formed by itself. But 'ḥak yerekhot', that is, engraving the parts of the letter and making them stand out, is considered writing, as they wrote on the tzitz: 'Holy to the Lord' by engraving the letters from its back side. And likewise we learned regarding the Tablets of the Covenant, that the writing was engraved on them and was considered writing (Tosafot there). On this basis many poskim wrote that relief printing, which is done like a seal by a person's hands, is considered writing valid for gittin and for STaM, since it is 'ḥak yerekhot'. And they further added the reasons brought above. So wrote the Masat Binyamin 99, the Taz (Oraḥ Ḥayim 284:2; Yoreh De'ah 271:8), the Divrei Ḥamudot (Tefillin 8:23), the Get Pashut (Even Ha-Ezer 125:15), the Shevut Ya'akov (1:15), the Penei Me'irot (1:45), the Mor U-Ketzi'a (Oraḥ Ḥayim 32), Responsa Maharatz Ḥayot (1:11), the Maharam Schick (Oraḥ Ḥayim 66) and the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (Yoreh De'ah 271:39; Even Ha-Ezer 125:37). And so wrote in our days Responsa Or Yitzḥak (Yoreh De'ah 53) regarding silk-screen printing. And some wrote that this is the basic law, but in practice one should be stringent: Responsa Maharam Provinzalo 73, Rema of Fano 93, the Magen Avraham (32:57; 284:1) and the Da'at Kohen 160.
On the other hand, many disqualified the use of printing for STaM, because writing is the scribe writing the letter with his hand, and even engraving the parts of the letter is done in a way that creates the letter by striking from the other side, and therefore is considered writing. Whereas a seal or printing is like sticking a picture onto the parchment, and this is a kind of grama. And they further added the reasons brought above. So wrote the Maharashdam (Yoreh De'ah 184), the Baḥ (Oraḥ Ḥayim 691:4), the Ḥavot Ya'ir 184, the Eliya Rabba (Oraḥ Ḥayim 691:5), the Benei Yona (the short version 271:25; and in the long version 5), the Zera Emet 2:117, the Birkei Yosef (Oraḥ Ḥayim 691:1), the Ikkarei Ha-Dat (Oraḥ Ḥayim 36:53), the Ḥatam Sofer (Gittin 20a), the Lishkat Ha-Sofer (28:2; 7), the Da'at Kedoshim (271:9), the Sefer STaM of Rabbi Shlomo Kluger 61, the Piskei Halakhot, the She'ilat David (part 1, siman 7), the Mishpetei Uziel 6:78 and the Yeḥaveh Da'at (6:57). And since the law is from the Torah, one must be stringent like them.

sections.title_en: 10. The Form of the Letter – the Kinds of Script
sections.body_en:
The scribe must be careful in writing the letters, that no letter be changed from its form or resemble another letter. Every letter has basic components, a change in which changes its form and invalidates it, and components intended to add beauty to it, whose absence does not change its form and does not invalidate it (as explained at length in the Beit Yosef and Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 36, and the Mishna Berura there).

There are three main customs in the form of the letters: the 'Beit Yosef' script (explained in the Beit Yosef, Oraḥ Ḥayim 36), which most of those of Ashkenazi origin follow. The Ari script, which most Ḥasidic groups follow. The Ari script is basically identical to the 'Beit Yosef' script, but it has slight changes in seven letters (alef, vav, ḥet, ayin, tzadi, final tzadi, shin). The third custom is the script followed by those of Sephardi origin (called 'Velish'), and it is a more rounded and less polished script. Therefore its writing takes less time, and accordingly its price is about a third lower than the other scripts.
