From the outset it is right for every person to continue in the custom of his forefathers, and to acquire a Torah scroll, tefillin and mezuzot according to their custom, but by the letter of the law one can fulfil the obligation with any of the scripts. Likewise, members of all communities are permitted to be called up to a Torah scroll in any of the kinds of script, and one who needs to put on his friend's tefillin may put on the tefillin of a member of another community with a blessing (see above 4:9, note 12).7

notes_en.en: A baraita (Shabbat 103b): "'And you shall write them' (Devarim 6:9) – that the writing be perfect: that he should not write alefs as ayins, ayins as alefs; bets as kafs, kafs as bets; gimels as tzadis, tzadis as gimels; dalets as reshes, reshes as dalets; hehs as ḥets, ḥets as hehs; vavs as yods, yods as vavs; zayins as nuns, nuns as zayins; tets as pehs, pehs as tets; bent letters as straight ones, straight ones as bent ones; mems as samekhs, samekhs as mems; closed ones as open ones, open ones as closed ones". The Rosh (Responsa 3:11) and the Me'iri (Kiryat Sefer 2:1) wrote that only what is mentioned in the baraita prevents validity, since by it one letter resembles another, but the differences between the customs of the communities are not included in this, and therefore Sephardim fulfil their obligation with the script of Ashkenazim and vice versa. And so emerges from the words of the Rambam (Laws of Torah Scroll 10:1, 15) and the Rashba (Ha-Ḥadashot 145). The Mahariksh explained (Ohalei Ya'akov 113): "Therefore they did not elaborate in their answers to teach the people of Israel the form of the letters". And the Maharḥu added in Sha'ar Ha-Kavanot in the name of the Ari (the matter of tefillin, end of discourse 2) that "all of them have an allusion and a secret alluded to above, for with several depictions and changes and combinations the forms of the letters change". And the Le-David Emet (13) brought this. On the other hand, the Birkei Yosef (Oraḥ Ḥayim 36:2) brought responsa of the Maharam ben Ḥaviv and the Mahari Molkho (from manuscript), that following the change in the form of the letters "tefillin of Ashkenazi script are invalid for Sephardim". And the Divrei Mordekhai (Oraḥ Ḥayim 143) inclined to this. It is reasonable that in their view Sephardi script too is invalid for an Ashkenazi. But the view of the overwhelming majority of the poskim is that all the scripts are valid for all communities; and so wrote the Maharam Galanti 124, the Ḥakham Tzvi 99, the Noda Bi-Yehuda (second edition, Yoreh De'ah 171), Rabbi Shlomo Kluger (Kin'at Soferim 161), the Ḥayim Be-Yad 83, the Maharsham (2:120; 7:112), the Ein Yitzḥak (1, Yoreh De'ah 28:15), the Yeḥaveh Da'at (2:3), and many others. And although for those of Ashkenazi origin the thorn of the 'yod' prevents validity, and in Sephardi script many are not particular about it, since there are several views in explaining the thorn of the 'yod', and in Sephardi script people follow some of those views, one should not invalidate it even for those of Ashkenazi origin, and when necessary those of Ashkenazi origin too can fulfil their obligation with it (Igrot Moshe, Oraḥ Ḥayim 5:2; Mitzvat Ha-Yom, p. 17).

sections.title_en: 11. Invalid Letters and Words, and Asking a Child
sections.body_en:
When one of the letters is invalid, the whole scroll or passage is invalid. There are three main kinds of invalidity in letters: the first, that one letter resembles another, and there are letters prone to this, such as vav–yod, vav–final nun, kaf–bet, dalet–resh, nun–gimel, nun–kaf, mem–final mem, samekh–final mem (Shabbat 103b). The second, that one of the basic parts of the letter is missing, even the thorn of a 'yod'. The third, a break between the components of the letter, such that a basic component of the letter has been cut off from its main body. One must pay particular attention that there not be a break in a letter composed of several parts, such as 'alef', 'shin', 'ayin'. On the other hand, there are two letters composed of two separate parts – 'heh' and 'kuf', and in them, if a join forms between the leg and the roof – they are invalid (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 36:2).

If a doubt arose regarding the form of a letter, for example the leg of a 'vav' is so short that perhaps it resembles a 'yod', or the roof and base of a 'nun' have lengthened until it perhaps resembles a 'kaf', one decides on the basis of 'asking a child', who is "neither clever nor foolish", and he determines which letter it is. That is, one asks a small child who is not clever, meaning that he does not know how to understand from the context which letter ought to be written there. And on the other hand, he is not foolish, for he already knows how to read the letters well, and will not mistakenly read a properly written letter as another letter. If he said the letter that ought to be there – it is valid, and if not – it is invalid (Menaḥot 29b). Since one asks a child who is not clever enough to understand the context, there is no need to cover the letters around the doubtful letter. When the form of the letter exists, but it was written not according to halakha, for example there is a break between the roof of the 'dalet' and its leg, one does not ask a child, for although the child will see that it is a 'dalet', since its parts are not joined – it is invalid (Shulḥan Arukh and Rema, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:16. And see Taz 32:10; Mishna Berura 51).

One must leave a space the size of a small letter (the letter 'yod') between word and word, so that it will be clear that these are two words. If the scribe erred and joined two words to each other until they look like one word, or left a space in the middle of a word until it looks like two words – it is invalid. And if there is doubt whether they look like two words or like one word, one performs 'asking a child': if he reads properly – it is valid, and if not – it is invalid (Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 274:4; Taz 2; Rema, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:32; Mishna Berura 143).8

notes_en.en: The source of the law of 'asking a child' is in Menaḥot (29b): "a child who is neither clever nor foolish", as explained above. Many hold that since he is not clever enough to understand the context, there is no need to cover the words around the doubtful letter (Levush 32:16; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 20; Kol Ya'akov 63, and others). And some say that it is preferable not to cover, lest as a result of the covering he err and invalidate it for nothing (Darkhei No'am, Even Ha-Ezer 3; Mikdash Me'at 32:57). And some say that one must cover the words before the doubtful letter, lest he understand from the context (Maharit, Yoreh De'ah 32; Halakhot Ketanot, part 1, 100; Magen Avraham 32:19; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 34; Mishna Berura 51). In the Keset Ha-Sofer (6:2) he wrote that by the letter of the law there is no need to cover, but people were accustomed to cover the letters before it. In Responsa Maharshag (1, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2) he explained that there is a concern lest the 'child' be clever, and therefore one covers in a Torah scroll. But in tefillin and mezuzot, which cannot be corrected if the child reads in a way that invalidates them, because of 'not in order', one may ask a minor without covering, according to the basic law.

sections.title_en: 12. Spaces and Being Surrounded by Parchment
sections.body_en:
The scribe must take care that every letter be surrounded by parchment on its four sides, that is, surrounded by the white of the gevil or kelaf on which it is written, and it is enough that there be between letter and letter a space like a hair's breadth. If a letter stuck to another, or reached the edge of the parchment, since in that place the letter is not surrounded by the white of the parchment – the scroll or the passage is invalid. But this can be corrected by scraping away the ink at the place of the join, or at the place where the letter touches the edge of the parchment, so that it will be 'surrounded by parchment'. And since even before the correction the form of the letter was there, this can be corrected even in tefillin and mezuzot 'not in order' (Menaḥot 29a; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:4; Yoreh De'ah 274:4; below halakha 15).

If there was a small hole in the parchment, and he wrote a letter that touches the hole, since at the point where it touches the hole it is not surrounded by the white of the parchment – it is invalid. And if he scraped the point of contact and now it is surrounded by parchment – it is valid. If after the writing a hole formed adjacent to a letter, since the letter was written validly – it is valid.9

There is an allusion in this halakha: the black letters express ideas that we know and understand and can explain, and therefore we are able to express them by means of letters. But there are sublime, lofty and deep ideas that no word or letter can contain or explain, and from them flow all our insights and thoughts. The white parchment surrounding every letter expresses those lofty ideas that cannot be expressed. And out of the white parchment, the black letter is revealed and appears before our eyes. Out of what is above consciousness, known and clear ideas are revealed to us. And this is the essence of the Torah: its source is heavenly and lofty, and it descends to us according to our understanding and to our everyday lives. In order to express this, every letter must be surrounded on all its sides by the white of the parchment (see Likkutei Torah of the Alter Rebbe, Shir Ha-Shirim 46c; Derekh Mitzvotekha of the Tzemaḥ Tzedek, the mitzva of tefillin 2).

notes_en.en:
Menaḥot (29a): "Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: Any letter that is not surrounded by parchment on its four sides – is invalid". The Beit Yosef asked (32:16): But we learned (Menaḥot 29b) that if the leg of the 'vav' in the word 'va-yaharog' was pierced and a child read it as 'vav' – it is valid; why did they not invalidate it on account of its not being surrounded by parchment? And he gave two answers: a) The invalidity of 'surrounded by parchment' applies only when a letter stuck to another, but a hole adjacent to a letter does not invalidate it, and so he inferred from Rashi. b) A hole invalidates on account of 'surrounded by parchment' only if it was there before the writing, but if the letter was written validly and afterwards a hole was made beside it, it is not invalidated on account of 'surrounded by parchment', for the law of 'surrounded by parchment' is learned from 'and you shall write them', that the writing be perfect – at the time of writing (Peri Megadim 32, Mishbetzot Zahav 8). And so the Beit Yosef learned from the Rambam. In practice the Shulḥan Arukh (Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:16) ruled stringently, that only when the hole was made after the writing is the letter valid. And even if the hole reached from letter to letter, according to many they are valid. But since there are those who invalidate in this case, one must correct them (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:15-16; Mishna Berura 34; 54).
Further in Menaḥot (29a): "Ashiyan bar Nadbakh said in the name of Rav Yehuda: If the inside of a 'heh' was pierced – it is valid". According to most Rishonim, he means that if the hole was in the inner part of a letter that has a hollow, like 'heh', 'kaf' and the like, even if it filled its whole inner hollow – it is valid, for the law of 'surrounded by parchment' does not apply to the inner hollow. On the other hand, according to the Yerushalmi (Megilla 1:9), also in the inner hollow it must be surrounded by parchment. In practice the Shulḥan Arukh (Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:15) wrote the view of the Bavli without attribution, and added: "But in the Yerushalmi it is implied that also on the inside it must be surrounded by parchment". And the Aḥaronim wrote that one should be concerned for the words of the Yerushalmi (the Baḥ, the Taz, the Peri Megadim, the Mishna Berura). The poskim disagreed whether the Yerushalmi invalidates only when the hole fills the whole hollow of the letter (Taz 32:8), or also part of it (Mishna Berura 37, and see Bei'ur Halakha, s.v. 'Aval bi-Yerushalmi'). And they likewise disagreed whether the Yerushalmi invalidates a hole even when it was made after the writing of the letter (see Taz 32:8; Noda Bi-Yehuda, first edition, Yoreh De'ah 75; Keset Ha-Sofer 7:7).

sections.body_en:
A Torah scroll, tefillin and a mezuza must be written by an act of writing and not by engraving, as it is said: "And you shall write them" (Devarim 6:9; 11:20), and the Sages expounded (Gittin 20a) on a similar case regarding a get: "And he shall write (Devarim 24:1) – and not engrave". Therefore, if a drop of ink fell on the parchment, and he engraved within it and around it until the form of a letter was created – it is invalid, for this is not writing but engraving, and this is 'ḥak tokhot' (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:17). Likewise, if a drop of ink fell on a letter, until its form is not recognisable, it is forbidden to correct the letter by erasing the superfluous ink; rather, he should erase the drop and then complete the missing part of the letter. Similarly, if he mistakenly wrote 'vav' instead of 'yod', it is not possible to validate the 'yod' by shortening the long leg of the 'vav'; rather, one must erase the whole 'vav' and write a 'yod' anew (Shulḥan Arukh there). And likewise if he mistakenly wrote 'dalet' instead of 'resh', it is forbidden to validate the 'resh' by erasing the superfluous part; rather, one must erase the whole of it and write it anew. If the leg of the 'kuf' or the 'heh' touched the roof of the letter – he should erase the leg and write it anew. This is the rule: every part that was written invalidly – requires erasing and writing anew. And in a letter that does not have two parts, the whole letter is considered as written invalidly (Shulḥan Arukh 32:17-18; Taz 17; Mishna Berura 75).

But if the invalidity is because two letters stuck to each other, if despite the contact between them the form of the letter is recognisable on them, they can be validated by erasing the point of contact. And this is not called 'ḥak tokhot', for only when the erasing creates the form of the letter is it invalid on account of 'ḥak tokhot', whereas here the form of the letters was recognisable even without the erasing (Shulḥan Arukh there 18; Mishna Berura 80). Even when the letters of God's Name stuck together, it is permitted to separate them, and there is no prohibition of erasing the Name in this, since he is thereby repairing it (Shulḥan Arukh there 26; Yoreh De'ah 276:11. But if they stuck together after the writing one should not separate them, Mishna Berura 32:126).

Sometimes mistakes occurred in writing the Torah scroll, and it was not possible to correct them by erasing, because many words would have had to be erased there. In these situations the solution is to cut out from the parchment the piece in which the mistake is, to stick in its place a piece of parchment (a patch) from below, and on the stuck-on parchment to write what is required without mistakes (Rema, Yoreh De'ah 280:1; Keset Ha-Sofer 18:4-5).

However, if the problem arose as a result of writing a holy Name in the wrong place, some say that out of respect for the Name – it is forbidden to cut it out (Rema 275:1; Shakh 3); rather, one must remove the whole sheet, which generally has about four columns, put it in geniza and write the required columns anew on a new sheet. And some say that in order to save the sheet from geniza, it is permitted to cut out the Name and put it in geniza (Taz, Yoreh De'ah 276:7; Naḥalat Shiv'a 37). In practice, when necessary people are accustomed to be lenient and cut out the parchment on which the Name is, together with a few more words as needed, and stick a patch of parchment there, and write on it properly (Benei Yona; Keset Ha-Sofer 11:8, 13; Lishkat Ha-Sofer 23). And the better one knows how to stick on the patch in a way that it knits together more beautifully with the parchment, the more one can rely on this advice.10

Some hold that when a mistake occurred in a holy Name, instead of cutting out the place of the Name together with more words, which is disputed, it is preferable to remove the Name by peeling it off. That is, an expert scribe removes the upper layer of the parchment with the Name written on it, and puts it in geniza, and so one can write on the parchment what is required (Responsa Mahari Le-Beit Levi 81; Beit David). And some hold that one should not do so, lest part of the Name be erased during the peeling. Further, perhaps this is considered like one who writes a scroll half on kelaf and half on dukhsustos, which is invalid. Further, there is a concern that the place on the parchment on which the Name was written has become sanctified and it is forbidden to write other words on it (Tosafot, Arakhin 6a, s.v. 'Yagod'; Tashbetz 1:149; Magen Avraham 32:26; Benei Yona; Keset Ha-Sofer 11:11). Today, expert scribes are accustomed to peel (Kol Ya'akov 276:28-29; and see Yeri'ot Shlomo 15, note 34). And many of those of Ashkenazi origin are not accustomed to peel.

If it became clear to the scribe that he forgot to write a word or several words in the Torah scroll, in the past people were accustomed to correct this by 'suspension' (tliya), that is, writing what was missing between the lines, above the place where the previous word ended (Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 276:1). And one must first score the place where the word is suspended (Keset Ha-Sofer 3:5. In tefillin and mezuzot suspension does not help, since they must be written in order).

However, in the days of the Aḥaronim people were accustomed not to suspend a word between the lines (Benei Yona 276:9; Lishkat Ha-Sofer 10:10). Likewise, in the past people were lenient, when necessary, to write a few letters outside the line, and in the days of the Aḥaronim they were accustomed not to do so (Responsa Ginat Veradim, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:4). And it seems that people became accustomed to be stringent about this in the days of the Aḥaronim because the basic rule of writing STaM is that the writing must be 'a perfect writing' (Menaḥot 34a), and after printing began to be used and people became accustomed to straight lines, writing between the columns or between the lines is not considered a perfect writing.

notes_en.en: Massekhet Soferim (5:1): "One who writes two holy Names (where one Name is required) – keeps the first and holds back the last" (that is, cuts it out). And so wrote the Beit Yosef (Yoreh De'ah 276:11) in the name of a responsum of the Rambam, that "he cuts out the Name", the second one, and so wrote the Tashbetz (1:149), the Taz (Yoreh De'ah 276:7), the Naḥalat Shiv'a 37, and others. On the other hand, in the Responsa of the Rosh (3:7) he wrote that "Heaven forbid that one should cut out the azkarot from the sheet. It is better that he remove the sheet and write another in its place". And so wrote his son in Responsa Zikhron Yehuda 3. And in Responsa Maharalbaḥ 2 he wrote that by the letter of the law it would seem to be permitted, but since the Rosh was stringent about this, one should be concerned for his view. And the Rema (Yoreh De'ah 275:1) wrote that one should not cut out the Name "and make holes in the sheet", "for this is not an enhancement" (Levush there). And according to the Shakh 3, the prohibition is on account of the honour of the Name and not the making of holes in the parchment. And according to the She'elat Ya'avetz (1:153), the prohibition on cutting out applies only when one cuts out the Name because of an invalidity not connected with the Name, but if the Name is what invalidates the Torah scroll, for example it was written twice, as brought in Massekhet Soferim – it is permitted, and it is good to cut out other words with it. And according to the Ḥatam Sofer (Yoreh De'ah 264; 272), in this case even the Rosh would agree that it is permitted. And the Benei Yona (Yoreh De'ah 276:31) and the Keset Ha-Sofer (11:8) wrote in practice that in a place where people were accustomed to cut out a superfluous Name together with additional words – they may continue in their custom.

sections.title_en: 15. In Order, in Tefillin and Mezuzot
sections.body_en:
The Torah established a special law for tefillin and mezuzot, that they must be written in the order in which they are written in the Torah, letter after letter, as it is said in the passage of 'Shema' (Devarim 6:6): "And these words, which I command you this day, shall be", "'shall be' – as they are they shall be", and without this they are invalid. Therefore, if he finished writing the passages and it became clear to him that he forgot to write one letter in the first passage, or wrote it not in its proper form, there is no way to correct this, since the correction would be made 'not in order'. Since the passages are invalid, they must be put in geniza, as the Sages said (Mekhilta of Rabbi Yishmael, Bo, parasha 18): "He writes them in order, and if he did not write them in order – they are to be put in geniza".

If he was writing the passages of tefillin or a mezuza and remembered in the middle of the writing that he had omitted one letter, if it is possible to erase all the letters he wrote after that letter, he should erase them and write the letter he omitted, and go back to write the letters from it onwards in order. But if in the meantime he wrote one of the holy Names, which it is forbidden to erase, the passage cannot be corrected and it requires geniza. Therefore, when the scribe comes to write a holy Name, he should go back and read everything he wrote since the previous holy Name, in order to check that no mistake occurred in what he wrote (Beit Yosef and Shulḥan Arukh 32:22).

The laws of 'in order' apply to tefillin and mezuzot only, but the letters of a Torah scroll and a Megillat Esther may be written from the outset not in order. And although the sanctity of a Torah scroll is greater than that of tefillin and a mezuza, the Torah did not trouble us to write the letters of the Torah scroll in order, for since it is long, it is almost impossible for no mistake to occur in it, and if it were forbidden to correct it, we would have no valid Torah scrolls (Radbaz 1:310; Ginat Veradim, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:4).

Besides the order of the letters in the passage, the care for order must also be in the order of writing the passages (see above 4:8, 10). Therefore, if the passage of 'Kadesh' of the head-tefillin, which is the first, became invalid, the three passages after it are also invalid, since it is not possible to write the passage of 'Kadesh' for them now. But if they find a passage of 'Kadesh' that was written on a date earlier than their writing, they can join the three passages to it.

If he wrote one letter not in its proper form, for example a 'shin' without one head, or the leg of the 'heh' joined the roof and it turned into a 'ḥet', or he wrote 'dalet' instead of writing 'resh', it is considered as though he did not write it, and therefore, in addition to this letter being invalid, everything written after it is also invalid. But if the form of the letter was on it, except that there is another invalidity in it, for example there is a thin break between the parts of the letter, but it is clear that its form is on it, or it stuck to another letter without their form being changed, he may correct it not in order (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:25; Mishna Berura 114). If he erred and wrote a superfluous letter at the beginning of a word or at its end, he can erase the superfluous letter and thereby validate the passage, since all the letters in it were written in order (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:22).

The Torah scroll is written in passages, between which there is a space the size of nine letters. This does not mean the weekly portions, but much smaller passages; there are passages that contain only one verse and some that contain many verses.

There are open passages and there are closed ones. Whether a passage is defined as open or closed is determined by the space before its beginning: a passage written after an open space is called 'open' (petuḥa), and a passage written after a closed space is called 'closed' (setuma). The space of an 'open' passage expresses a greater break than the space of a 'closed' one (see Responsa Maharshal 37). In Ḥumashim an open passage is marked by the letter 'peh' before it, and a closed one by the letter 'samekh' before it. The Sages said: "And what purpose did the breaks serve? To give Moshe space to reflect between passage and passage and between subject and subject" (Sifra, Dibbura de-Nedava 1:9; 5:1).

The Rambam and the Rosh disagreed about several forms of space, whether they are considered an open or a closed passage, but there is a form that is agreed upon by all, and in this form people are accustomed to write Torah scrolls, so that they will be valid according to both views (Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 275:1-2). The agreed form: an open passage begins at the beginning of the line, and a closed one in the middle of the line.
That is, in order to make an open passage, one ends the one before it in the middle of the line, leaves a space the size of nine letters or more, and begins the open passage at the beginning of the next line. Like this:

[Diagram: an open passage]

In order to make a closed passage, one ends the previous passage at the beginning of the line or in its middle, leaves a space the size of nine letters or more, and begins the closed passage on that same line. So the space between the passages is closed on both its sides. Like this:

[Diagram: a closed passage]

According to what we learned (in halakha 12), that the white parchment alludes to the upper and hidden world from which flow the ideas that are revealed to us in the letters of the Torah, it is understood that before each and every passage there is a greater illumination and inspiration, which finds expression in the space before it. And there are two kinds of illumination, for an open passage and for a closed passage, and out of that illumination the next passage is revealed to us.

If he erred and made a passage break in a place not designated for it, or did not make a break where there is a passage, or made the break of an open passage in place of a closed one or a closed one in place of an open one – it is invalid. In order for the scribe to succeed in making all the passages according to this form agreed upon by both views, there is an order of writing ('tikkun soferim') that shows which words will be written on each line of the Torah scroll, in such a way that all the passages will be written according to both views. But a scribe who did not succeed in arranging his writing so that the passages will be according to both views should follow the view of the Rambam, according to which the halakha is ruled (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:36; Rema, Yoreh De'ah 275:2. See above 4:8 for how one acts in tefillin).11

notes_en.en:
Shabbat (103b): "An open passage – one should not make it closed, a closed one – one should not make it open". According to the Rambam (Laws of Torah Scroll 8:1-2), an open passage begins at the beginning of the line, and a closed one in its middle. And according to the Rosh (Laws of Torah Scroll 13), an open passage is a passage that has an open space before it, whether from the middle of the line to its end or from the beginning of the line to its middle, and a closed one is where the space is closed between the words on the same line, or where there is a whole empty line that is 'closed' between two full lines. It follows that when the previous passage ended at the end of a line, and the next passage must be made closed, according to the Rambam one must begin the next passage in the middle of the line (and so one does in tefillin, where the fourth passage must be closed), but according to the Rosh, if one does so it will be an open passage (since the space is open from the beginning of the line); rather, one must leave a space of a whole line and begin at the beginning of the third line. And if the previous passage ended at the end of a line, and the next passage must be made open, according to the Rambam one must leave a break of a line and begin the passage at the beginning of the line, but according to the Rosh, if one does so it will be a closed passage, and in order to make it open one must leave a space of nine letters at the beginning of the line.
If the previous passage ended in the middle of the line and a closed passage must be begun, but there is no room there for a space of nine letters plus a word for the beginning of the closed passage, according to the Rambam he should leave at the beginning of the next line a space of nine letters and begin the closed passage, and according to the Rosh he should leave a space of a whole line, and begin the next passage at the beginning of the third line. According to the Rosh the space in a closed passage must be at least about three letters, and according to the Rambam nine letters, and so is the halakha (Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 275:2).

sections.body_en:
There are two songs in the Torah that must be written with large and special spaces between the words – the Song of the Sea and the Song of Ha'azinu. In the Song of the Sea the writing is 'a half-brick over a whole brick', that is, on one line there are two spaces between the sections, on the line below it one space, and on the line below it two again, and so on (except for the first line, which is ordinary). In the Song of Ha'azinu the writing is 'a half-brick over a half-brick and a whole brick over a whole brick', with the writing on both sides of the line and the space in the middle (Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 275:4-5).

[Diagram: the layout of the Song of the Sea]

[Diagram: the layout of the Song of Ha'azinu]

In the Prophets and the Writings there are many more songs; some of them are written in the form of the Song of the Sea, such as the Song of Devora (Shofetim 5); and some of them are written in the form of the Song of Ha'azinu, such as the list of the thirty-one kings of Canaan (Yehoshua 12) and the ten sons of Haman (Ester 9), which are also songs (Megilla 16b). And some say that the whole book of Tehillim too is written like the Song of Ha'azinu.

According to what we learned (halakha 12), the space expresses the upper inspiration that surrounds our thought from above. And since the song comes to express a very lofty idea, there is a need for many systematic spaces within the writing, which express the upper inspiration from which the song flows.

If the scribe deviated and wrote the song like other writing, or wrote the rest of the Torah the way a song is written – the scroll is invalid (Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 275:3).

The tradition of the Written Torah includes four components. The first is the letters of the Torah, and as we learned (in halakha 11), if he changed the writing of one of the letters of the Torah, the whole scroll is invalid.

The second component is the crowns (tagin), which are three tiny, thin lines with a small circle at their top, in the shape of a small letter 'zayin'. The crowns adorn the tops of seven letters: sha'atnez getz (shin, ayin, tet, nun, zayin, gimel, tzadi). The Sages said (Menaḥot 29b): "When Moshe ascended on high, he found the Holy One, blessed be He, sitting and tying crowns to the letters. He said before Him: Master of the Universe, who is holding You back? He said to him: There is a man who is destined to live at the end of many generations, and Akiva ben Yosef is his name, who is destined to expound on each and every thorn (each crown) heaps and heaps of laws". The crowns are added to the roof of each of these letters, and when there are two roofs – to its left roof, with one crown leaning to the right, one to the left and the third in the middle, in this way:

[Diagram: the seven letters sha'atnez getz with their three crowns]

If he forgot and did not write the crowns, some say that the letter is invalid (Rabbeinu Tam, the Tur and the Baḥ), and according to many it is valid after the fact (the Rambam, the Me'iri and Rabbeinu Yeruḥam). And so is the halakha, except that one must hurry to add the missing crowns, and they may be added in tefillin and mezuzot even 'not in order' (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 36:3; Mishna Berura 15).

There are further letters that scribes are accustomed, according to the Kabbala, to crown with one crown, and they are bedek ḥaya (bet, dalet, kuf, ḥet, yod, heh), like this:

[Diagram: the letters bedek ḥaya with one crown each]

And if he did not crown them, all agree that the scroll is valid. The rest of the letters, which are the letters of

[Diagram: the letters of the phrase melekhet sofer (mem, lamed, alef, kaf, tav, samekh, vav, peh, resh)]

are not crowned at all.12

The two further components are the vowels and the cantillation marks (te'amim), which help in reading the Torah and thereby interpret its meaning. As a rule, the vowels interpret the meaning of the words, and the cantillation marks the meaning of the verses. The Sages expounded on the verse describing the reading of Ezra the Scribe (Neḥemya 8:8): "And they read in the book, in the Torah of God, distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading". "'And caused them to understand the reading' – these are the divisions of the cantillation". And some say: "these are the masorot", that is, the vowels according to which one reads (Megilla 3a).

The vowels and the cantillation marks are not written in the Torah, and they belong to the 'Oral Torah'. According to the wisdom of the Kabbala, the vowels and the cantillation marks allude to lofty and deep matters. And precisely because their root is in concealed and hidden worlds – they are not written in the 'Written Torah' (see Nefesh Ha-Ḥayim 2:16).

After the destruction of the Second Temple, the Sages permitted writing the Oral Torah, and included in this they permitted writing Ḥumashim with vowels and cantillation marks. But they do not have the status of the Written Torah, and one does not read from them in the Torah reading, and therefore one is also not particular to write them on parchment and in STaM letters (above 8:8-9).

notes_en.en:
Menaḥot (29b): "Rava said: Seven letters require three crowns, and these are they: sha'atnez getz". Some Rishonim hold that the crowns prevent the validity of the letter. Among them: Rabbeinu Tam, the Teruma, the Or Zarua, the Tur (Yoreh De'ah 274:6, in the name of the Rosh), the Baḥ (36:5) and the Eliya Zuta 3. On the other hand, according to most poskim, from the outset one must crown, but the absence of the crowns does not invalidate. So wrote Rav Sar Shalom Gaon (Sha'arei Teshuva 331), the Rambam (Responsa 154), the Ḥinukh, Rabbeinu Yeruḥam (Toledot Adam Ve-Ḥava 2:2) and in the name of Rav Hai Gaon, the Me'iri and the Tashbetz. And so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh (Oraḥ Ḥayim 36:3), the Ḥida (Tov Ayin 18:26), the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (36:3), and many others (see Yabi'a Omer 9, Yoreh De'ah 20). And since it can be corrected, many wrote that one should be concerned for the stringent views and add the crowns (Le-David Emet 11:17; Mishna Berura 36:15; Kol Ya'akov 36:18). In the Tikkunei Zohar Ḥadash (part 2, 96b) it is explained that the crowns on the letters bedek ḥaya and sha'atnez getz are "like a man who holds weapons in his hand and swings them to the right and to the left" (and see Nahar Shalom 33:2; Etz Ḥayim, Sha'ar Ha-Nekudot 6; Mishna Berura 36:15).
There is a further tradition from Ezra the Scribe to write dots above several words in the Torah, such as above "for us and for our children" (Devarim 29:28), and one should not invalidate a scroll that lacks these dots, although one must correct it and complete them (Taz 274:7). There is a further tradition of writing certain letters large or small, such as the 'bet' of "Bereshit", at the opening of the Torah, which is large, or the 'alef' of "Va-yikra", which is small. And likewise in the verse "Shema' Yisrael Hashem Elokeinu Hashem Eḥad" (Devarim 6:4), the 'ayin' and the 'dalet' are large. But if he did not do so – the scroll is valid (Keset Ha-Sofer 16:4). There are further traditions in writing the Torah, such as the broken 'vav' in the word "shalom" (Bamidbar 25:12; Kiddushin 66b), or the inverted nun (Shabbat 115b; Keset Ha-Sofer 16:7-8), and this is not the place to detail them. See the Tikkun Ha-Soferim at the end of the book Keset Ha-Sofer.

sections.title_en: 19. Marking the Cantillation in the Torah Scroll
sections.body_en:
The Torah scroll must be written without vowels or cantillation marks or punctuation marks, according to the tradition of its giving at Sinai, for in this way the Torah can be expounded in seventy facets. And if he wrote vowels or cantillation marks or punctuation marks in it – the scroll is invalid. Sometimes there is even a difference between the meaning of the written tradition (masoret) and the meaning of the reading (mikra) according to the 'Oral Torah', and each of the meanings has importance. For example, in the Torah scroll 'ba-sukkat' (Vayikra 23:42) is written, in the singular, but the tradition of vocalisation is to read it 'ba-sukkot', in the plural, and an important halakha is learned from the written tradition (Sukka 6b). One who writes the Torah with vowels cannot correct it by erasing the vowels, for by vocalising its words he demonstrated that he intended to write it for the sake of reading according to the 'Oral Torah' alone, and not for the sake of the tradition of the 'Written Torah', and therefore all his writing is invalid for a Torah scroll (Beit Yosef and Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 274:7; Taz 6).

One who reads the Torah in public must read with the cantillation, which helps in understanding the verse; one must especially be careful about the cantillation mark at the end of the verse, a change in which is liable to change the meaning (below 15:16). In order to make it easier for those reading the Torah, there were scribes who were accustomed to leave slightly more space between verse and verse than between word and word, and there were some in Ashkenaz who even recommended doing so (Rema, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:32; Shakh, Yoreh De'ah 274:6). On the other hand, many hold that although one should not invalidate a scroll in which slightly more space was left between verse and verse, from the outset one must keep, also between verse and verse, the fixed space that is between word and word, and so is the custom (the Rivash 286; Magen Avraham 32:45; the Gra 32; Mishna Berura 146, and others).

There are places where people were accustomed to incise marks in the parchment, in order to mark with them a number of cantillation marks. According to most poskim, from the outset one should not read from these scrolls, since some say that incising invalidates like marking with ink, but in a pressing situation one may rely on those who hold that its law is like a superfluous space, which does not invalidate. And in Yemen people were accustomed to read from them from the outset.13

notes_en.en: The custom of incising the parchment for the purpose of marking is accepted among many of the immigrants from Yemen, and its source is ancient. And so they were accustomed from the outset, as explained in Responsa Revid Ha-Zahav 29, and by Rav Kafiḥ in his commentary on the Rambam (Laws of Torah Scroll 11:11). On the other hand, among members of other communities, many invalidate a scroll in which punctuation marks were incised (Beit David, Yoreh De'ah 136; Ketav Sofer, Yoreh De'ah 142; Ein Yitzḥak, Yoreh De'ah 27). In the Igrot Moshe (Yoreh De'ah 3:117) he wrote that the immigrants from Yemen may continue in their custom. And in the Yeḥaveh Da'at (6:54) he wrote that after the fact they may continue in their custom, combined with the view that it is permitted to read from an invalid scroll. Thus far. In practice, since there is an important tradition that validates these Torah scrolls, the immigrants from Yemen may decide whether to continue in their custom or to be stringent so as to fulfil their obligation according to all the poskim. Guests staying at a Yemenite synagogue should follow the custom of the place, be called up to the Torah and recite the blessing over the Torah scroll.

sections.title_en: 20. The Beauty of the Writing and the Sewing of the Scroll
sections.body_en:
The Sages established rules in writing the Torah scroll, which are intended for the design of the writing and the relations between the script and the column and the parchment as a whole: the line must be of medium length, not too narrow, like a letter, and not too wide, so that the reader's eyes will not wander over the script and become confused between the lines. The Sages estimated that in fine writing the length of the line should be enough to write 'le-mishpeḥoteikhem' in it three times, that is, thirty letters in three words (Menaḥot 30a; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 272:2). When one writes in a thick script, the line may be longer, for there is no concern that they will be confused between the lines (Tosafot, Menaḥot there, s.v. 'Kegon'; Shakh, Yoreh De'ah 272:3).

The distance between line and line is the size of one line. From the top of the parchment to the beginning of the writing – the size of three fingerbreadths (about 6 cm), and from the end of the writing to the bottom of the parchment – four fingerbreadths (about 8 cm). Between column and column – two fingerbreadths (about 4 cm), and between book and book – a space of four empty lines. These rules are for the choicest performance of the mitzva, and if he deviated from them – it is valid (Menaḥot 30a; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 273:1, 5). One aims to finish the Torah scroll in the middle of the line at the end of the column (Menaḥot 30a; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 272:4).

Sometimes the scribe did not plan his writing correctly, and was forced to go beyond the limits of the column's end line, and then he is permitted to write a few letters outside the column's end line, and the poskim disagreed about the details of the permission. After the fact, if he wrote outside the column more than they permitted, as long as it appears that what he wrote is the continuation of the line and does not belong to the line in the next column, it is valid (Menaḥot 30a-b; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 273:3-4; Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:33-34; Mishna Berura 150; Keset Ha-Sofer 15:5). With the holy Names one must take care that not even one letter goes outside the column's end line. After the fact, even if he wrote the whole Name outside the end line – it is valid (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:35; Mishna Berura 154). Today people are accustomed to enhance and be particular about straightening the lines, and it is not common to write even one letter outside the line or to end the line one letter before its end line (above halakha 14).

It is a law given to Moshe at Sinai that the sheets of the Torah scroll are sewn with the sinews of a kosher domestic or wild animal (Massekhet Soferim 1:1). In order to beautify the scroll one sews on the outside, so that the one reading the Torah does not see the stitches (Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 278:1). The Torah must be whole, as it is said (Tehillim 19:8): "The Torah of the Lord is perfect, restoring the soul", and therefore only when the scroll is all sewn together does it have the sanctity of a Torah scroll and is read from in public. But if one sheet is not sewn, even though it is there, the scroll is invalid (Shulḥan Arukh there 4).

It is a beauty for the scroll that each sheet have four or five columns, and at least three columns, and at most eight columns. This is because the sheets are joined to one another by sewing, and it is not a beauty for the scroll to have too many or too few stitchings. After the fact, even if he made one column on a sheet, or more than eight – it is valid (Menaḥot 30a; Maharam Mintz 12; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 272:3; Taz 4; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 10).

The beginning and the end of the Torah are sewn to the rollers by which the scroll is rolled and held (Bava Batra 14a). These rollers are called 'atzei ḥayim' after the verse (Mishlei 3:18): "It is a tree of life (etz ḥayim) to those who hold fast to it". The custom of most of those of Sephardi and Yemenite origin is to place the scroll inside a beautiful case designated for the Torah scroll.

sections.title_en: 21. Proofreading STaM, and the Law of a Scroll That Became Invalid
sections.body_en:
The Sages said that it is forbidden for a person to keep in his house a scroll that has an error in it for more than thirty days, lest he forget and not correct it, and the error in it remain and take root. Rather, he should correct the scroll or put it in geniza, as it is said (Iyov 11:14): "and let not iniquity dwell in your tents" (Ketubot 19b; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 279:1). But if the invalid Torah scroll is marked, it is permitted to keep it for more than thirty days (Shulḥan Gavoha, Yoreh De'ah 279:1; above 9:13).

Since it is forbidden to keep a scroll that has an error in it, after the scribe has finished writing the Torah scroll he must hand it over for proofreading, for it is common for mistakes to occur in writing. In the past an expert proofreader would go over the scroll thoroughly and correct it of errors. When they saw that sometimes errors escape the proofreader's eyes, in many places they instituted that several proofreaders go over the scroll. And some were accustomed to fine a proofreader who did not find the errors.

About forty years ago a computer program was developed that scans photographs of the columns of the Torah scroll and finds errors in them. Following this, the ability to identify errors greatly improved, and today it is accepted to make use of the computer for proofreading Torah scrolls. In practice it is customary to carry out two computer proofreadings. After the first computer proofreading one corrects the errors the computer found, and proofreads again by computer in order to make sure that all the errors were properly corrected, and in order to give backing to the first proofreading. Besides this, an expert proofreader goes over the Torah scroll with a settled mind and with seriousness, and makes sure that it is written properly. And some are particular that two proofreaders proofread the scroll, for sometimes what one finds the other does not find. Tefillin and mezuzot, since they are short and the scribes know their passages well, by the letter of the law, if the scribe went over them thoroughly and proofread them, there is no obligation to have them proofread by a proofreader (Mikdash Me'at 279:35), but it is customary to hand them too to a proofreader, for sometimes an expert proofreader succeeds in noticing defects that escaped the scribe's eyes.14

notes_en.en:
Ketubot (19b): "A scroll that is not proofread – Rabbi Ami said: up to thirty days it is permitted to keep it, from then on it is forbidden to keep it, because it is said: let not iniquity dwell in your tents". The Rishonim there explained that it refers to a Torah scroll in which an error was found, and it is forbidden to keep it thirty days without correcting it (Rashi and the Shita Mekubetzet there; Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, Toledot Adam Ve-Ḥava 2:2; the Tur, Yoreh De'ah 279:1). This implies that if no error was found in it, there is no obligation to check it. And so it is implied by the Rashba (7:287), that only if three errors were found in the scroll is it forbidden to read from it until the whole of it is proofread. But on the other hand, the Rashba wrote (1:1056) that "there is no scribe who is so precise in his writing that he does not err at all". This implies that one should not read from a Torah scroll that has not been proofread. And so wrote the Benei Yona (Yoreh De'ah 279:11), and in the long part there (7) he gave the reason: "for our eyes see that many errors are common in this work". And so it is implied by the Mikdash Me'at (there 35) and the Shulḥan Gavoha (there 1). And so wrote the Beit Shlomo (STaM 142), the Ḥesed Le-Avraham (Yoreh De'ah 86:2) and the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (279:15). And in the Kol Ya'akov (Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:115) he wrote that in Baghdad they instituted four proofreadings by four people. On the other hand, according to the Ḥatam Sofer (Zer Soferim, Ateret Zekenim 2), the Ḥiddushei Ha-Rim (279:1) and Responsa Lehorot Natan (6, Oraḥ Ḥayim 1), by the letter of the law, when the scribe has the reputation of being God-fearing, and he went over the scroll and found no mistakes in it, there is no obligation to proofread it before reading from it. But even according to their view, people are accustomed to be stringent and proofread it. Today the prevalent custom is that one does not read from a Torah scroll that has not been properly proofread.
Computer proofreading: around the year 5747 (1987) a dedicated computer program for proofreading STaM was developed. In the Shevet Ha-Levi (7:2) he encouraged checking by means of it, because it turned out that the computer succeeded in identifying errors that proofreaders had not discovered. However, he emphasised that one must also proofread by means of a person, for sometimes the computer did not succeed in distinguishing between the letters, and did not find all the errors. And some were concerned about using computer proofreading lest people rely on it and become lax in the proofreading done by a person, and so it would turn out that people would read from scrolls with errors (Minḥat Yitzḥak 10:89). And some were concerned about adding computer proofreading because it would cast aspersions on earlier generations who did not use it (Mishneh Halakhot 11:114). Over time the proofreading program became more sophisticated and it became clearly evident that it is beneficial, until the great majority of halakhic authorities agreed that it is right to carry out a double computer proofreading, as brought above. Nevertheless, experience has shown that in the meantime computer checking does not perfectly replace human proofreading in finding defects in the form of the letter, joins and the like, and therefore it is agreed that a meticulous human proofreading is also required, as explained above.
